questions.stem: What are the four main components of blood?

options.text: Red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, plasma

questions.explanation: Blood is made up of plasma (liquid component), red blood cells (carry oxygen), white blood cells (fight infection), and platelets (help with clotting).

questions.stem: What is the function of plasma?

options.text: To transport dissolved substances such as glucose, hormones, CO2, and urea

questions.explanation: Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid that makes up about 55% of blood. It transports dissolved substances including glucose, amino acids, hormones, urea, and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: What protein do red blood cells contain?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that binds with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin, transporting oxygen to body tissues.

questions.stem: How do white blood cells defend the body against infection?

options.text: By phagocytosis (engulfing pathogens) and producing antibodies

questions.explanation: White blood cells defend the body by phagocytosis (engulfing and destroying pathogens) and by producing antibodies and antitoxins that target specific pathogens.

questions.stem: What is the role of platelets?

options.text: To help blood clotting at wound sites to prevent blood loss and infection

questions.explanation: Platelets are cell fragments that play a crucial role in blood clotting. At wound sites, they help form a network of fibrin fibres that creates a clot, preventing blood loss and pathogen entry.

questions.stem: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?

options.text: To make more room for haemoglobin, allowing them to carry more oxygen

questions.explanation: Red blood cells lose their nucleus during development to create more space for haemoglobin. This allows each cell to carry the maximum amount of oxygen.

questions.stem: How is carbon dioxide mainly transported in the blood?

options.text: Dissolved in plasma as bicarbonate ions

questions.explanation: Most carbon dioxide (about 70%) is transported dissolved in the plasma as hydrogen carbonate (bicarbonate) ions. Some is carried bound to haemoglobin and some dissolved directly in plasma.
